‘The Visage of Offence’: A Psychoanalytical View of Forgiveness and Repentance in Shakespeare's Plays

Bernardine Bishop

Bernardine Bishop

7 Patshull Road, London NW5 2JX. [email: bernardinebishop@yahoo.co.uk]

Bernardine Bishop  

This paper attempts to explore some aspects of the psychological effort and achievement that constitutes the nature of forgiveness. It looks at forgiveness through the lens of different emotional processes shown in Shakespeare's plays. It aims to trace some lines of development in Shakespeare's thought. It argues that both forgiveness and repentance are hard-won and precarious psychic states, and that both call for considerable struggle and pain. It suggests that shallower and less evolved states of mind may sometimes masquerade as forgiveness and as repentance, and that there are certain spurious short cuts to both. Shakespeare reflects both authentic and inauthentic forgiveness and repentance at various moments in his plays.

Inpatient Psychotherapy and Prenatal Regression

Philippe Ployé

Philippe Ployé

rachelwinterbjp@aol.com.

Philippe Ployé  

Prenatal forms of regression are not often talked or written about, even in discussions or works concerned with inpatient psychotherapy. This is strange considering that life in hospital is particularly apt to induce such regressions and that, as far back as 1929, Simmel had already pointed out that patients treated in hospital ‘by psychoanalysis’ tended to ‘identify their life in the clinic … with the hidden intra-uterine existence’ (Simmel 1929, p. 86). It is suggested that if and when these forms of regression come to be better explored and understood, one way of dealing with them could be to use a modified form of the already well-known and ‘bipolar’ type of staff structure in which the difficulties which patients' acting out between sessions often creates for the nursing staff are attended to by a member of staff other than the therapist himself.

Sex and Sexuality: Winnicottian Perspectives edited by Lesley Caldwell. Published by Karnac, London, 2005; 179 pp; £19.99 paperback.

Jane Cheshire

Jane Cheshire

Jane Cheshire  

This book is the most recent volume of the Winnicott Studies Monograph Series. It is the third to be edited by Lesley Caldwell and with its exciting title appears to open a fresh line of thinking about Winnicott.

My understanding of Winnicott's work has been that it is centred on what is needed for human individuality to be sustainable. It tends to bypass the impact of sexual difference, the significance of the Oedipus complex, the role of the father, and the significance of sexuality and the drives. Instead, much of his focus is on the prerequisites for ‘in-dwelling’, the location of the self in a body, with the possibility of a unit self, of integration and de-integration, made possible by maternal preoccupation and early care-giving. Without this, instinctual experiences and demands can never be other than overwhelming. This work privileges infantile experience and the role of the mother in early life as the central predictive indicator for mental well-being. Despite his idiosyncratic style these preoccupations situate Winnicott within the British tradition of psychoanalytic thought, rooted in empiricism and humanism. His observations of thousands of mothers and children in his paediatric work, his accounts of his psychoanalytic work with his patients, and some of theirs of being analysed by him provide a unique record of his central concerns: feeling real, psyche-soma, being able to play and so on.

The cover blurb says that ‘His writings contain unexplored insights into sexuality and it is these hidden insights that prompted Lesley Caldwell to invite papers from leading analysts to expand upon them’. And it is true that she has gathered some very eminent contributors for this book - Mario Bertolini, Lesley Caldwell, Andreas Giannakoulas, André Green, Joyce McDougall, Francesca Neri, Adam Phillips, Helen Taylor Robinson, Dominique Scarfone and Maggie Schaedel.

In her introduction Lesley Caldwell makes no mention of how the book came into being. It isn't clear whether she had invited papers specifically on Winnicottian perspectives on sexuality or whether these papers had been more loosely collected under the theme. Her introduction begins with an acknowledgement that sex and sexuality are not ‘an integral part of Winnicott's concerns’ (p. 1). She describes the articles collected in the volume as ‘attentive to sexuality - particularly infantile sexuality’ as they explore a ‘Winnicott unapologetically linked to Freud and to a psychoanalysis located in the drives’ (p. 2). Perhaps this wording allows for sufficient leeway as several authors explore themes other than sexuality (often very interestingly). I was left unsure about whether there just wasn't very much to say on the subject of Winnicott and sexuality or whether something was being evaded.

Analytic Intuition: A Meeting Place for Jung and Bion

Sherly Williams

Sherly Williams

Bedford MK43 7DB. [email: sherly.williams@ukonline.co.uk]

Sherly Williams  

The paper identifies some important areas of theoretical congruence between Jung and Bion in order to illuminate a central feature of analytic practice: analytic intuition. Jung and Bion suggest, in different yet surprisingly similar ways, that the therapist extends her reach towards unknown psychic reality through the exercise of analytic intuition. Both writers invite us to respect the symbolic and relational processes by which painful and disturbing emotional reality is intuited. Their particular formulations of unconscious process are used to arrive at a definition of analytic intuition and how it is experienced and used by analytic practitioners. The paper discusses Jung's and Bion's understanding of the dreaming process and also makes reference to Bion's ‘reversible perspective’ and Jung's ‘synchronicity’ as particular ways in which analytic intuition can be employed in analytic interpretation. The paper concludes by drawing a parallel between Jung's ‘transcendent function’ and Bion's ‘binocular vision’.

A Case Study of Power and the Eroticized Transference-Counterfransference

Joseph Newirth

This study of power in the eroticized transference-countertransference presents two sessions in the middle stage of an analysis of a woman struggling with issues of anxiety about her own power and a belief that her love and desires are destructive, toxic and murderous. The case is presented from a neo-Kleinian/relational perspective in which the analytic strategy focuses on the development of enactments and transitional experiences and the use of evocative, presentational language, in contrast to a more traditional interpretive strategy in which discursive language concentrates on historical explanation and the differentiation of fantasy and reality. The two contiguous sessions begin with the patient's concerns about the bad behavior of the analyst and his male colleagues at an institute group-process conference. These reservations reflect the patient's anxieties about potential destructiveness and aggression, her resentment about the unfairness of men's sense of social and professional privilege, and the use of sexuality to dominate and control others. The analysand initially presents her concerns in an abstract, intellectualized, impersonal manner with little affect or connection between external events and her internal world.

As the first session progresses, the patient's concerns become articulated in more personal affective forms reflecting the dynamics of a highly eroticized transference-countertransference relationship that is articulated as the patient's identification with a powerful woman and the fantasy of raping the analyst and the subsequent paranoid anxieties about being attacked by a female boss. The second session works through the issues of power and the eroticized transference-countertransference through the development of the patient's unconscious fantasies and beliefs that her loving and desirous feelings will be destructive, leading to loss, disappearance and murder.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Rachel Winter

Rachel Winter

[rachelwinterbjp@aol.com]

Rachel Winter  

Freud's analytic couch is one of the most famous pieces of furniture in the world, both feared and revered as a metonymic image of the psychoanalytic process. For visitors to the Freud Museum in London, it is an object of fascination. Everyone longs to lie on it. And yet one is always struck by its homeliness. It is a typical domestic divan of its time, nothing special; a scroll-ended couch upholstered in plain beige cloth. These divans were intended to be covered, perhaps with velvet cloth or, as here, with a rug. The rug is a Qasqa'i, made in Iran. There are embroidered and deep-pile velvet cushions heaped on it. Above it hangs a lithograph of the painting Une Leçon Clinique à la Salpêtrière by André Brouillet (1857-1914), showing Charcot displaying to colleagues his patient Blanche Wittman, in a state of hypnosis. The general effect is a blend of the domestic and the clinical. Before Freud, the patient's life and illness were kept separate and patients were seen solely as objects of study by the doctor. By listening to his patients, Freud linked their subjective experiences to the objective moment of therapy. The fact that dreams and everyday matters were the currency of this treatment made it accessible to everyone.

He listened to them; he made them physically comfortable, he sat out of sight to help maintain some emotional distance but also because he didn't want to be stared at all day long; as he grew older post-operative infections damaged his hearing on the right side so that he had to reverse the position of the couch and chair in order to hear his patients. Thus the analytic couch is both a powerful symbol and a useful reminder of Freud's and his patients' human realities.

Throughout 2006, which brings the 150th anniversary of Freud's birth, we shall be publishing a number of papers inspired by Freud and his work and we welcome further contributions to this.

The papers in this issue reflect some of the variety of our mutual endeavour, the inheritance of the couch, still bringing together the subjective and objective, on the couch or off, mainstream or maverick, in the continuing attempt to know the unknowable.

Hate and the ‘Jewish Science’: Anti-Semitism, Nazism and Psychoanalysis by Stephen Frosh. Published by Palgrave/Macmillan, London and New York, 2005; 228 pp; £25.00.

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz

London

Joseph Schwartz  

Stephen Frosh has assembled a powerful and important book analysing racism. His purpose is not academic but practical; an attempt to provide a psychological and social analysis that can be an effective tool in the essential battle against racism. In his words:

[This book] is psychosocial arguing that it is artificial to separate psychological from social processes, and that they have to be understood as entwined with one another, so that the deep feelings which people often take to be aspects of their ‘identities’ are connected in innumerable ways with the social and cultural forces out of which they arise. It is also a polemical book, based on the belief that there is nothing more dangerous in contemporary society than racism, and that studies of racist ideas and actions - here in the specific guise of anti-Semitism - continue to be necessary as part of the essential task of combating racism wherever it is found. (p. 5)

Frosh uses the Nazi persecution of psychoanalysis as a ‘Jewish Science’ as an extended case naturally of relevance to psychotherapists.

Editorial

Rachel Winter

Rachel Winter

[rachelwinterbjp@aol.com]

Rachel Winter  

I am writing this on the anniversary of the London bombings of 7 July 2005. My consulting room is by a church in the City of London, close to Aldgate Underground Station, the site of one of the explosions. The church, St Botolph's-Without-Aldgate, acted as the emergency control centre in the first hours after the blast and for the next 10 days and 10 nights gave support and shelter to the emergency services working in the tunnel. St Botolph is the patron saint of travellers and this church, appropriately, stands on an island where eight roads meet. As it stood outside the city gate, it also became known as the Outsiders' Church, ministering to the homeless, the outcast and the forsaken. There has been a church of this name on this site for almost a thousand years, through wars, plague and fire. Today it is the container for a huge outpouring of emotions. The churchyard is full of flowers and all day hundreds of City workers have been going in and out, the church bell tolls, people stand together in the street and cry. Inside is an exhibition of paintings by Vaseem Mohammed, a young local Muslim artist. His paintings fuse Christian and Islamic symbolism with his personal associations. The exhibition is entitled ‘Unity’.

I wrote in my last editorial about how difficult it can be to hold what we have in common in the face of what divides us. Today in my room by the church, I am thinking about this yet again and about loss and grief, terror and rage, grievance and vengefulness, hope and reconciliation.

Many of these are involved in the complex and difficult matter of forgiveness. In this issue we publish three conference papers under the title ‘Forgiveness: Is It Really Possible?’. David Black introduces the section and asks a number of pertinent questions: is forgiveness common or is it rare? Is it desirable? What does it mean? Does it ever happen? Does it involve a betrayal of the past and of our grief for a future that will never now happen?

Chris MacKenna brings together psychotherapeutic and religious thinking and suggests that forgiveness necessitates the achievement of a ‘third position’ within ourselves.

Celia Downes

Celia Downes

London

Celia Downes  

Clare Winnicott had a seemingly inexhaustible fund of stories; here is the story of how she and Donald first met. In 1941, during the Second World War, Clare Britton, aged 35, had recently completed the psychodynamically based Mental Health Course for social workers at the London School of Economics and was working in the Midlands for the Regional Health Authority. Donald Winnicott was making weekly visits as consultant psychiatrist to five hostels set up in Oxfordshire to house young evacuees who were too disturbed to be billeted out into private homes. Clare recalls her briefing from her boss: ‘There's a difficult doctor working in that area. He comes down once a week. He doesn't believe in social work, because he likes to do it all himself. But it's really in quite a mess, and you must go and straighten the whole thing up’ (pp. 128-9).

Clare's approach to the task is a model for psychotherapists working as community based consultants. The staff were frustrated that Dr Winnicott was not telling them what to do. Clare suggested: ‘Well, let's never ask him what to do. Let's do the best we can in the present situation, and then, when he comes again, tell him what we did and see if he's got any comments to make on it and if we can therefore learn something from what we did’ (p. 129). Not content with enabling both the hostel staff and Winnicott to form an effective working relationship with each other at one remove from the children, Clare saw there was more to be done to shift Dr Winnicott into a more appropriate and effective position: 'One thing I did was to stop him eating all the children's rations in one meal!

Influential Papers from the 1920s (International Journal of Psychoanalysis Key Papers Series) edited by R.D. Hinshelwood. Published by Karnac, London; 280 pp; £19.99 paperback.

James Park

James Park

London [james@antidote.org.uk]

James Park  

‘The great dissensions are little addressed’, says editor Bob Hinshelwood in his introduction to this selection of papers from the International Journal of Psychoanalysis during the 1920s. This rather glosses over the point that the purpose of the journal in its first decade, under the editorship of Ernest Jones, was to show a professional community working collaboratively together to elaborate its theories, apply them to clinical practice and resolve in the process their intellectual conflicts.

Hinshelwood's collection includes excerpts from the debates on how to analyse children that involved Hermine Hug-Hellmuth, Melanie Klein and Anna Freud; papers by Joan Rivière and Karen Horney challenging the accounts men had offered of women's inner worlds. There is also an analysis by Edward Glover of Sándor Ferenczi's proposed modifications to psychoanalytic technique, and Jones's own quizzical look at the superego, Freud's latest idea at the time.

There are several dangers in reading these papers with the hindsight provided by the years that have elapsed since they were written. One is that we end up viewing them through the eyes of the conflicts that were to come in the following decade. As a result, we uncover signs that Ferenczi was itching to start his withering denunciations of the classical analytical position in his Secret Diary; the first rumblings of the rancorous discord that provoked the Controversial Discussions between followers of Anna Freud or Melanie Klein; Karen Horney taking the first steps that led to her joining the other ‘interpersonalists’ as they quit the American Psychoanalytic Association in the late 1930s.

The second danger follows from this - that we fail to give credit to the intellectual struggle involved in forging the cogent arguments presented on these pages. Reading, for example, Ferenczi's 1926 paper on ‘The problem of acceptance of unpleasant ideas’, it is easy to see it as a rather unsatisfactory adumbration of the ideas that we know of as Margaret Mahler's separation-individuation model and Klein's depressive position, rather than as a pioneering piece of work in its own right. Having the benefit of exposure to later conceptualizations makes it hard to embrace some of these writers' intellectual worlds. I, for one, will never get my head around Karl Abraham's argument on ‘the influence of oral erotism on character formation’. It is just too far away from how I have learned to think.

Editorial

Rachel Winter

Rachel Winter

[rachelwinterbjp@aol.com]

Rachel Winter  

In 1984 when Bob Hinshelwood had the idea of starting a journal to represent the many different, sometimes opposing, voices in British psychoanalytic psychotherapy, he invited a number of organizations to become involved. Six organizations accepted this challenge. They worked out a deal by which all their members would subscribe to the Journal at a greatly reduced rate and the Editorial Board would comprise representatives from every Sponsoring Organization. This meant that they all had a hand in the Journal and shared the responsibility for its future.

That unwritten contract was symbolic of the spirit of ecumenism that lay at the heart of the enterprise. The task was and is to struggle against polarizing processes and repeatedly renew co-operative communication. The Journal has grown well beyond its local origins and is now read by thousands of clinicians across the world, but its roots lie in British psychoanalytic psychotherapy and its discontents, its historical tensions and divisions.

The attempt to hold what we have in common in the face of what divides us is a tough project and perhaps it will never get any easier. Yet I believe, as I imagine those founding fathers believed, that it is important to keep talking, stay involved, win a little, lose a little. It is encouraging to receive so many messages of appreciation from admirers of the Journal. But also and inevitably, from time to time its Sponsoring Organizations have expressed various dissatisfactions. The Journal is in thrall to psychoanalysis, not psychoanalytic enough, too broad based, too obvious, too recondite and so on. Such differing views are hard to integrate. In the very first BJP editorial there is mention of a ‘swaying edifice of acrobats’ and I am often reminded of the phrase.

Bob Hinshelwood told me recently that all the Chairs involved in those early days were enormously supportive of the aims of the new venture, but of all of them, the most supportive and most enthusiastic was Lionel Monteith, the founder in 1967 of the Lincoln Clinic and Centre for Psychotherapy. So it is particularly sad that after 22 years the Lincoln has decided to withdraw from the field of dreams, or give up the fight, whichever applies.

Why Love Matters: How Affection Shapes the Baby's Brain by Sue Gerhardt. Published by Brunner-Routledge, Hove and New York, 2004; 246 pp; £9.99 paperback.

Carol Broughton

Carol Broughton

London

Carol Broughton  

This is a timely book with what might be construed as an ironic title - why do we need proof that love matters? Freud (1914) in his paper ‘On narcissism’ came to the conclusion that without love the human psyche was condemned to sterile self-obsession. Freud, in fact, receives short shrift in Gerhardt's book and there are frequent somewhat dismissive references to the Freudian project, as if all the new science that she quotes renders him obsolete. She states that ‘… unlike Freud, who searched beneath the surface of personality for the primal drives, the sexual and aggressive urges that he felt were the unseen motors of human life’, she looks instead ‘for the unseen patterns of relationship that are woven into our body and brain in babyhood’ (Gerhardt, p. 13). In fact, it could be argued that what we now know of the surprising capacity of the infant to communicate with others from the moment of birth contrasts profoundly with Freud's view of ‘his majesty the baby’, the embodiment of his parents' narcissistic investment. It might be interesting later in the review to consider whether Freud does still have relevance in view of recent findings in neuroscience.

Gerhardt's main concern in this book, however, is to draw together recent work in neuroscience and attachment research in order to argue for the importance of early affective experience in sculpting the newborn brain and in creating subsequent attachment patterns. In this respect, her book adds valuable weight to the argument for more investment in early infancy and in supporting parents in the work of loving and caring for their babies. Gerhardt includes a number of quotes from the feminist literature which are very moving, describing the struggles of mothers to care for their infants through moments of exhaustion and despair, sometimes losing a sense of themselves in the process, yet with a fierce pride and love for their babies: ‘To be a mother I must leave the telephone unanswered, work undone, arrangements unmet. To be myself I must let the baby cry, must forestall her hunger or leave her for evenings out, must forget her in order to think about other things. To succeed in being one means to fail at being the other’ (Cusk 2001, quoted in Gerhardt, pp. 75-6). Again there is little sense of ‘his majesty the baby’ in these quotes. They are important, too, in the context of the debate about child-care and the right of women to return to work. Some of the work in the field of mother-infant attachment (see, for example, Belsky & Fearon 2002) has been seen by some as anti-feminist, putting women back in the home, denying their freedom to be themselves, to make their own choices over child-care.

European Journal of Psychotherapy, Counselling and Health7(3), 125-136, 2005

Shattering the Subject: Georges Bataille and the Limits of Therapy

Benjamin Noys

This article is an analysis of the work of the French intellectual Georges Bataille (1897-1962) and its implications for interrogating the limits of therapy. One of the central concepts of Bataille's thought is transgression and the destabilizing effects of transgression on any concept of the limit. I explore this thinking through an analysis of Bataille's personal and theoretical relationship to psychoanalysis. Bataille's radicalization of psychoanalysis is then pursued through his use of mythic representations of the ‘shattered subject’. These models of the shattered subject offer an interrogation of some of the theoretical and practical limits of therapy, particularly when it is centred on the individual. Drawing on these models it is then argued that Bataille offers a new ethics of abjection, which proposes that we must interrogate the subject in terms of what our culture regards as ‘waste’. Comparison is made between Bataille's thought and that of Jacques Lacan, and it is argued that Bataille offers a potential radicalization of Lacan's concept of the Real and his ‘ethics of psychoanalysis’. The limits of Bataille's own writing are critically interrogated, drawing on the readings of his work by Jacques Derrida and Michel Foucault.



European Journal of Psychotherapy, Counselling and Health7(3), 143-157, 2005

The Way of Authenticity and the Quest for Personal Integrity

M. Guy Thompson

The author reviews the respective conceptions of authenticity proposed by the existentialist philosophers, Friedrich Nietzsche and Martin Heidegger, each of whom situate it in the inherent difficulty of resisting the herd instinct in one's interpersonal relationships, then sets out to show how, despite the absence of authenticity as a technical term in the psychoanalytical lexicon, the technical principles of psychoanalysis enumerated by Freud are compatible with the views of Nietzsche and Heidegger. The author then gives examples of other psychoanalytic authors who similarly embrace the spirit of authentic relating in their conception of the clinical situation, including the work of D.W. Winnicott, Wilfred Bion and Jacques Lacan. The author concludes that in the psychoanalytic context the imposition and experience of suffering are invaluable components of authenticity and therapeutic change.

Schreber's Fall

Paul Zeal

Paul Zeal

12 Elm Grove, Taunton, Somerset TA1 1EG. [email: paul.zeal@btinternet.com]

Paul Zeal  

Schreber and Freud never met. This gives Freud the freedom to interpret without having to contend with Schreber's reactions. This paper explores connections and disconnections between their two texts. Both men are attempting to work out the place of the feminine in a man, one from a position of masculine collapse, the other from a position of masculine strength. Unheard, Schreber became increasingly woebegone and strident until, with the help of his memoir as a self-object, he began to reintegrate. Freud, on the other hand, well heard in his psychoanalytic fraternity, could venture an at the time seemingly unchallengeable reading of Schreber's memoir. Since 1911 a considerable literature has accumulated, analysing Schreber and reinterpreting Freud, and this paper briefly considers some of the main and divergent strands, and includes a response to the mystical in Schreber.

A Final Note: A Pivotal Moment

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

This is a personal moment for me. The Journal has been an important thing which I am proud of. When I started it with a small band of colleagues from the six original organisations which founded the Journal in 1984, I could not have imagined it to have developed into the player it has become. So passing it on to a new owner is a big thing. I have thought to myself it is like choosing a boarding school for my child - or arranging a marriage for a daughter. Quite impossible tasks!

The Journal started as a very small idea and was quite remarkably successful from the very first issue - which had to be very quickly reprinted. And that powerful support for the Journal has carried it through many difficulties since - not least the division of our world into the UKCP and BCP as it was. I can't count all the people who have contributed in all sorts of ways to the success of the Journal over more than two decades. So I should give a generic thank you to all of you, to everyone past and present, rather than invidiously selecting some rather than others. It is simply the case that the Journal has been the product of very many dedicated people and is no way my creation, even though I had a founding hand in it.

Although the Journal was never a direct component of the identity of British psychotherapy, it has been very central in supporting that identity. I remember when I was setting up the Journal, one of the very first subscribers wrote on the subscription form that ‘It is about time we had an organ of our own!’ I have always been spurred on by that sense of the psychotherapy profession needing a boost to its potency. And have always wanted the Journal to contribute to that seminal function. I believe it has born real fruit, and must continue to do so.

However, now the important thing for me is to recognise that I have given up my stake in the future. However tempting it is, nobody has a right to reach beyond the grave as it were and seek to go on influencing the future. So it is for an owner relinquishing the title. It is the right time for me to pass this venture on.

Confidentiality: A Contribution to the Debate

Anne Gray

Anne Gray

19 Kingsbury Avenue, St Albans, Herts AL3 4TA. [email: gray330@btinternet.com]

Anne Gray  

A ‘Clinical Conversation about Confidentiality’ between Lesley Mur din and Julian Stern was presented in Clinical Commentary XXXIV (BJP 21(4)). Dialogue was placed at the heart of that commentary, the conversational format reflecting the dialogue between those involved. It was conceived as a way of breaking out of the practitioners' isolation within the consulting room. This was part of a strategy to involve the reader more in the clinical commentary. So the Clinical Commentary Editors for the ‘Conversation’ were pleased that the following piece has arisen as a further contribution to the debate.

Sue Robinson

Jan Lee

The recent publication in the Clinical Commentary series, ‘A Clinical Conversation about Confidentiality’, prompts this contribution to the debate. Using the concept of absolute confidentiality, advocated by Bollas and Sundelson in their book The New Informants (1995), I look at the arguments for this stance and then draw attention to difficulties and contradictions in taking this position. I end by making a plea for uncertainty and all the anxieties inherent in not having absolute answers to questions of ethics.

The Nature of Psychoanalysis

There is more agreement about the similarities of psychoanalysis with analytic psychotherapy than there is over what differentiates these ways of working. Use of the couch, number of sessions per week, depth of work, training of the practitioner; all these factors come into the picture. However, the concept of the unconscious as a way of thinking about the communications made by patients is particular to both and differentiates these practices from other therapies.

Nick Barwick

Nick Barwick

London

Nick Barwick  

Anecdote is never the best source of evidence. In terms of credibility, it features lower even than ‘expert opinion’. Nevertheless, I have noticed, in conversations with colleagues (particularly those working with adolescents and young adults), just how frequent presentations of self-harm have become.

What seems evident from anecdote is soon borne out by evidence of a ‘harder’ kind. For example, an interim report from the National Inquiry into Self-Harm published in September 2004 highlights Childline's own records: an increase of 65% in calls relating to self-harm in the last two years and an average increase of 23% per year over the last ten. According to the Mental Health Foundation, in 2003, 24,000 teenagers attended hospital having deliberately self-harmed - mostly cutting, burning, severely scratching, biting, scalding, poisoning themselves, or pulling out their hair. Further, the Samaritans report that the number of young men presenting with self-harm has doubled over the last 10 years, while a YWCA briefing to the Oxford Monitoring System reported an increase of 70% overall over the same period. Whether these dramatic rises are due to an increase in occurrence or disclosure is debatable. Yet, whatever the reason, if the nature of self-harm were not alarming enough, the fact that those self-harming are, according to recent research, one hundred times more likely to commit suicide, forces the point even more sharply home.

In this context, Maggie Turp's Hidden Self-Harm: Narratives from Psychotherapy is particularly well timed and the surge of interest that it has stimulated amongst counselling and therapy organizations and colleagues (I recently witnessed a workshop she gave at a national conference where the numbers swelled from the proposed couple of dozen to more like a hundred) only too significant. The intense need (and greed) for insights into ways of working with ‘self-harmers’ is both apt and entirely in keeping with Turp's essentially object relations approach.

Sue Robinson  

I have always enjoyed the publications from the Cassel (such as Tom Main's ‘The ailment’ (1957) and Kennedy et al.'s The Family as Inpatient (1986)). This book edited by Lesley Day and Denis Flynn was no exception. Their title describes their work as ‘collaborative therapeutic care’, which presupposed a question for me about the feasibility of such collaboration between professionals working in different settings from the Cassel. Coombe, in one of the early chapters in the book, speaks of this collaboration as a ‘function of the institution as a container’ and he says, ‘A fundamental and vital feature of the Cassel treatment is the provision of containing structures…. These are multiple, and they extend far beyond the therapist-patient relations. It includes the existence, on a daily basis, of relationships of differing quality with groups and individuals allowing the holding and evolution of conflictual states of mind’ (p. 5).

Coombe's and Dowling's early chapters provide illuminating and thought-provoking accounts about work with different family members in a case of Munchausen syndrome by proxy. Coombe focuses on the way joint supervision with the psychosocial nurse and the mother enabled him to be aware of how he might ‘annihilate the child from his awareness’. Dowling, working with the poisoned girl, supplies the suggestion that one account of this syndrome can be depicted as ‘illnesses and injuries … used by parents, particularly the mother, to get attention for their own distress’ (p. 15).

Day, in her introduction, described their ‘work as a “landmark” case, showing the possibility of personality shifts in a parent with this diagnosis, previously deemed “untreatable”’. Day highlights the paucity of resources available for psychotherapy with adolescents in her introduction and explains that the Cassel provides a ‘last resort’ service at tier 4. This led me to reflect on ways in which clinicians, not at the cutting edge of a ‘last resort service’ but at levels 2 and 3, or even in sectors outside the NHS (such as the voluntary sector, the collaborative agency services or the private fostering agencies), might use the work of the Cassel to learn ways to close the gaps in helping distressed adolescents find containment in the existing services.

Dear Professor Freud…

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

38 Berkeley Road, London N8 8RU. [email: a.sabbadini@googlemail.com]

Andrea Sabbadini  

London, 6 May 2006

Dear Professor Freud,

To the memory of my father, Emilio (1911-2004)

The rich correspondence you have entertained with your colleagues throughout your life has encouraged me to overcome my initial reserve and address myself to you to wish you a happy birthday.

My choice of the two words preceding your name, Dear Professor, is not coincidental - indeed, as you have taught us, not much ever is. The Dear stands for my affection for you, or at least for what you have come to represent for me - and I am sure this is coloured by idealization and projections of all sorts. In a word, by my transference to you as it has evolved in the many years that I have been in contact with your ideas, studying and later teaching your texts, practising your theories in my clinical work as well as applying them to my understanding of the personal lives of myself and of those around me.

Associated to this word ‘Dear’ there is also for me a private memory, distant but still crystal-clear (or so I want to believe), which I would like to share with you. I was about 5 or 6 years old and my father was away from home for a period. My mother had convinced me to write a letter to him - and there she was, as so often in my childhood, sitting next to me to try and help me. As I wrote Caro papà, she insisted that I should replace the Caro with the superlative form Carissimo. I refused. ‘Dearest’ being a longer word to write than ‘Dear’, she decided that my disobedience must have been a symptom of my laziness. Yet I believe (or, perhaps, I just want to believe) that I was already aware then that my reluctance was not - or, better, not only - the sign of a limitation in my character, and certainly not of a limitation in my love for my dearest father, but of something else

ANDREA SABBADINI, C.Psychol. is a psychoanalyst in private practice, Honorary Senior Lecturer at University College London, Book Review Editor of the International Journal of Psychoanalysis, and Chairman of the European Psychoanalytic Film Festival. Freud's paper on the Schreber Case is considered from a contemporary perspective drawing on the object relations theorists. Some of Winnicott's ideas are used to illustrate how one might understand Schreber's predicament today. Although Freud's views on the role of repressed homosexual longings in the aetiology of Schreber's illness are not endorsed his prescience in the search for meaning in the patient's discourse is applauded.

Subject to Change is a collection of essays spanning a 20-year period of theorizing and practice by the renowned Jungian analyst and academic. The diverse ideas and perspectives discussed in these essays deal with the big issues relating to how Jungian analysts and psychoanalysts understand their profession and what it teaches us about our subjective lives. The book is divided into four sections: (1) Subjectivity and Uncertainty; (2) Gender and Desire; (3) Transference and Transformation; and (4) Transcendence and Subjectivity.

‘These essays will have’, so claims the book's cover, ‘significant appeal to all those concerned with Jungian analysis, psychotherapy, psychoanalysis, gender development and the interface between psychotherapy and spirituality’. This is indeed a considerable claim. Can it be justified? I think the answer is unquestionably in the affirmative as Young-Eisendrath's probing, open-minded intelligence, humanity and integrity suffuse every page where she invites the reader to engage challengingly and creatively with her ideas. Because the essays that make up this book cover around 20 years of her life it effectively serves as an autobiographical account of her intellectual and professional development as Jungian analyst, Buddhist and feminist.

Section 1: Subjectivity and Uncertainty is probably the most important of the four as it sets out most of the author's key ideas.

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander  

Arriving just before the 150th anniversary of Freud's birth, this amazing book tries something quite new by using an ingenious method which systematically covers the entire range of Freud's writings. It fills the gaps left by previous attempts at annotating, analysing and introducing Freud's monumental works, like J. Laplanche and J.P. Pontalis' The Language of

524

Psychoanalysis, C. Rycroft's Dictionary of Psychoanalysis and scores of Freud biographies and histories of psychoanalysis. Jean-Michel Quinodoz, Swiss analyst and author of the book, explains that it evolved from a seminar on the reading of Freud's texts for training analysts that he has been running over a period of years, which involves the active participation of its members. He calls his approach to the seminar ‘chronological, correlative and interactive’, as it enriches the reading and discussion by placing the texts chronologically in their historical and biographical contexts, showing how Freud's thinking and his concepts developed over the years, adding the main post-Freudian developments of psychoanalysis, and introducing biographies of immediate disciples together with those of major figures in psychoanalysis who succeeded Freud. In Quinodoz's words, he has adopted ‘an international approach with the aim of highlighting the diversity of contemporary thinking among analysts who are members of the International Psychoanalytical Association’.

The layout and structure of this reader-friendly book are highly original, introducing highlighting and colour-coding, the use of many different fonts and styles for chapter headings and sub-headings, including extensive quotes and mini-biographies, separating a section called ‘Discovering the text’ in each chapter from sections called ‘Post-Freudians’ and ‘New concepts’ and meticulously referencing and annotating every text individually. The book deliberately uses the words of everyday language, as Freud did in German which in no way diminished the complexity of his thinking. All this makes for a rich reading experience with briefings on each chosen text, amplified by comments, reflections, relevant biographical and historical material, all of which can lead to a good understanding of the unfolding process of Freud's thinking over four decades.

Many readers of the BJP will be aware that Bob Hinshelwood has been considering selling the Journal for a while now. In June this year the British Association of Psychotherapists (BAP) and Blackwell Publishing made a joint offer to buy the Journal and, after a meeting with Bob Hinshelwood and with representatives of the Sponsoring Organisations, this offer was accepted and the contracts were signed in August this year.

We are aware that there will be a variety of opinions about this change in ownership given the history of political debate and conflict within our profession over the years. The BAP is an organisation of three sections - Psychoanalytic, Jungian Analytic and Child and Adolescent - and we therefore have considerable experience of containing a variety of theoretical positions and occasional, inevitable conflicts under one roof. The BJP has always had the vital role of providing a forum for the different voices within the profession of psychoanalytic psychotherapy in the UK. These are voices which come from both UKCP and BPC organisations and the BAP and Blackwell Publishing are fully committed to continuing this policy.

The BAP has published its own Journal for more than 40 years and so has never been a Sponsoring Organisation of the BJP. The JBAP is published twice yearly and is read by members of the BAP as part of their subscription, as well as by a small external readership. We have been aware over the last year or so that journal publishing is changing rapidly and that those such as the JBAP and the BJP need to go on-line and be available to reach an international readership if they are to survive. From the point of view of the Council of the BAP, our offer to purchase the BJP was made in the light of the many similarities in the editorial policies of the BJP and the JBAP making it possible to combine the two. What Blackwell Publishing offers in particular is to provide the expertise, software and experience to place the combined journal on the international stage and thus increase its circulation, readership and influence.

Chairman's Introduction

David Black

David Black

[dmblack@clara.co.uk]

David Black  

If you do a quick trawl through the indexes of Freud, Klein, Ernest Jones, Bion, etc, you will find not a single entry for forgiveness. So it is not a word that has been given the splash of paint that Winnicott once said turns an ordinary word into a psychoanalytic technical term. Nevertheless, psychoanalysis has taken a detailed interest in many of the concepts to which forgiveness centrally relates, for example, trauma, grievance, resentment, vengefulness, hatred, guilt and shame. If I may venture to guess at the attitude of my colleagues, I think they would likely agree that forgiveness is a very important notion, but would hesitate to use the word for fear of seeming to underestimate its complexity and difficulty.

In religious traditions, by contrast, particularly in Christianity, forgiveness is spoken of a great deal. The central prayer of Christianity says: Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those that trespass against us, as if ‘we’, if we are ordinary decent people, are forever and without too much trouble forgiving the people who offend us. For those brought up with this traditional religious language, it can come as quite a shock to encounter the bitter, relentless tenacity of deep-seated grievance, the single-minded hatred and sense of irreparable loss that fuels passionate vengefulness.

So one question we might ask about forgiveness is: is it common, or is it rare? In one sense, if we are to be social beings, we do indeed have to forgive one another frequently. Contrary to Winnicott's encouraging phrase, parents are never good enough; nor are our lovers, spouses, friends, teachers, children or psychoanalysts. We have to forgive them abundantly if we are to love them and not fall ill. And we have to forgive ourselves too, if we are to play these important roles with any reliability. We are here in the familiar psychoanalytic territory of narcissism and the depressive position.

Common sense might expect us to make a distinction between two sorts of trauma, the more or less predictable and the outrageous.

Emma Letley  

The outcome of therapy is always to some extent determined by the first session, its nature and success. Freud himself attached considerable importance to the start of the treatment. Lesley Murdin's Setting Out comprehensively considers issues and debates around the subject addressing both experienced clinicians and students of psychotherapy and counselling.

Chapter one, ‘In the Beginning Was the Word’ makes the book's position clear. Beginnings in therapy are vital; after all, some prospective patients will attend for only one session, leaving the issue of what they will take away with them as a most pertinent question. In the early sessions, for those who stay, most would agree that the main role of the therapist is to listen attentively and actively. The patient may need to see current relationships in terms of her/his originary myth; and an appropriate question at the assessment stage may be, ‘How do you think your parents felt about your birth?’ (Later the authors advise the therapist also to attend to her own myth of origin.)

One way of beginning is with phenomenology; each model has some kind of developmental theory from Freudian fixation points, through Jung's archetypes, to twenty-first century writers' updating of the archetype through knowledge of genetics. The patient comes to therapy with some patterning, with certain responses to a new situation inbuilt. The writers enjoin the competent contemporary therapist to be informed about current developments in information theory, genetics and neuroscience. The clinician should not, it is stressed, be alone in her endeavours but should have a supervisor or consultant and make her work visible to another.

Chapter two addresses ‘The Birth of a Narrative Self, the coming, in Lacanian terms, into 'full speech’. Apart from Lacan, however, there is a dearth of literature on language development. This is linked possibly with the Kleinian emphasis on projective identification. As a culture we seem fascinated in this century by autism as the great popularity of Luke Jackson's and Mark Haddon's books (2002 and 2003) bears witness. Both show that the dilemma of finding the right words is an essential task not just for adolescents but for the adolescent self within the adult. Gregory Bateson (1979) has said that we think in stories: for therapy to begin the patient must be able to articulate her/his story.

Susan Budd

Susan Budd

London

Susan Budd  

Periodic attempts have been made by various philosophers to show that psychoanalysis is either valid or invalid. They may be interested in the theory of mind, or the puzzle of mind-body relations, or consciousness, or person-hood, or the nature and limits of scientific enquiry, or the hermeneutic nature of knowledge. We clinicians generally react by bending lower over our lasts.

Lavinia Gomez has bravely taken on the task of trying to compare three philosophers' views of the epistemological basis of psychoanalysis. She bases her selection on one of the Freud Wars, a series of skirmishes which break out periodically in the New York Review of Books. This particular skirmish was begun in 1993 by Frederick Crews, a professor of literature who dismissed psychoanalysis as a vast con trick, supporting his criticisms by the work of Adolf Grunbaum, a philosopher of science, who considered psychoanalysis to be nonscientific. Thomas Nagel, amongst others, contributed to the debate. Nagel argued that psychoanalysis is a successful empirical science, which has transformed our view of what a person is. Neither Nagel nor Grunbaum considered whether or not psychoanalysis should be classified as a science, whereas Jürgen Habermas considered it not to be a science, but a hermeneutic endeavour.

The second part of the book can be simply described. It consists of three excerpts from the work of these philosophers. Adolf Grunbaum's ‘Critique of psychoanalysis’ from The Freud Encyclopaedia of 2002; Thomas Nagel's ‘Freud's permanent revolution’, a 1994 review in the New York Review of Books of a book by Richard Wollheim, with an addendum which is his riposte to Grunbaum's reply to his review; and Jürgen Habermas' ‘The scientistic self-misunderstanding of metapsychology: on the logic of general interpretation’, which is a chapter taken from his Knowledge and Human Interests of 1971. Whilst all three papers are interesting, and well chosen from the point of view of showing the structure of the differences between them over the nature of psychoanalysis, I found myself wondering whether Lavinia Gomez had not been too modest in leaving them to speak for themselves, rather than inserting a more detailed consideration of their arguments into her chapters 2-4, where she analyses and discusses each philosopher in turn.

This book follows an earlier volume, Supervising Psychotherapy, by the same editors and again offers a selection of chapters, each addressing a separate theme in supervisory work. Where the first book is a valuable text for beginner supervisors, as well as being useful to practising supervisors, the new volume is a more demanding read and there is less emphasis on practical application.

A skilful opening chapter by Edward Martin on the unconscious makes Matte Blanco's ideas accessible for those who find them useful, if not rendering them appealing to all readers. His other chapter is on shame and uses scriptural myths to consider how shame arises essentially from separation anxiety. He distinguishes eloquently between the experiences of shame and guilt before giving a case example from a supervisory group, where fear of shame prevented a neophyte therapist from thinking about erotic counter-transference and a boundary violation.

The Last Farthing

Chris MacKenna

Chris MacKenna

17 Marylebone Road, London NW1 5LT. [email: cmackenna@stmarylebone.org]

Chris MacKenna  

Forgiveness is powerfully enjoined within the Christian tradition, but how feasible is forgiveness and what are the consequences of non-forgiveness? This paper explores these questions by considering the therapeutic experiences of three people for whom forgiveness was an issue. Their struggles suggest that part of the process of forgiveness may be working towards a ‘third position’, within ourselves, which transcends the instinct to portray our relationship with the person who has hurt us in terms of absolute goodness or badness, innocence or guilt. The significance of the ‘third position’ is that it provides a way of ‘seeing’ ourselves as we were at the time of the outrage, and the person who hurt us as they were at that time, and of continuing to live with both, while not being controlled by either. This understanding of forgiveness is then set alongside the experiences of two people who showed a remarkable capacity to use this ‘third position’; and also the author's experience, as priest and therapist, of hearing confessions which have arisen out of therapeutic work.

This paper addresses a very familiar subject, with a particular focus on the psychotherapist's contribution to the transference-countertransference unconscious dynamic. It summarizes some of the many discussions on counter-transference drawing from the vast literature on the subject. A case study is also given to illustrate the concept in clinical practice. The paper returns to the literature to trace the key elements that characterize it, and highlights the reiteration of different formulations of the same basic ideas. It then moves on to wonder about the reasons for this abundance of literature, proposing a parallel between the unravelling of countertransference in psychotherapy and the creative act, both based on the experience of personal discovery, where the production of an artefact does not require new subject matter but a fresh and personal reinterpretation.

Introduction

Muriel Brown

Muriel Brown

Muriel Brown  

‘Reconsidering Schreber: Contemporary Perspectives’ was the title of a Study Day held at the Severnside Institute for Psychotherapy in July 2005. The idea came from one of the Study Day Committee members, David Pocock, who wrote inviting two other SIP members, Sue Gottlieb and Paul Zeal, and myself to prepare short papers reconsidering Freud's paper, ‘Psychoanalytic Notes on an Autobiographical Account of a Case of Paranoia’ (Freud 1911) which was based on Schreber's Memoirs of My Nervous Illness (Schreber 1903), from a contemporary perspective.

The Study Day Committee had thought of using different psychoanalytical views on a single case, similar to the Journal's Clinical Commentary approach, but starting with Freud's paper as case material. It was hoped that the three speakers would cover a range of ideas from contemporary Freudian, Kleinian and Independent traditions, and we were invited to reappraise Freud's theorizing and go beyond his material, particularly into the biographical detail on Schreber now available.

The three invited speakers engaged with the task in very different ways, reflecting their different theoretical orientations but also drawing on their reading and on their clinical and life experience, to prepare papers which would open up the study topic. Sue Gottlieb followed Freud's recommendation that his readers ‘make themselves acquainted with the book by reading it through at least once beforehand’ (Freud 1911, p. 140). She became immersed in the Memoirs and decided to try to understand Schreber for herself, using only the same source material that he had. Paul Zeal also returned to source, and to Freud, and then considered Schreber's material in Lacanian and existential perspectives, reviewing the fate of devalued and misunderstood femininity. I found myself drawn to re-reading various other bits of Freud's own works, and biographies, as though getting alongside him, before turning to consider Schreber's predicament from an Independent view.

The papers, ably introduced by the Chair, Herbert Hahn, provoked a response that was thoughtful in an academic sense but also deeply empathic and emotional. There was much feeling for Schreber the man as members explored the tragedy of his breakdown and pondered the many factors that might have contributed to it.

London

John Skitt  

A member of the Independent Group within the British Psychoanalytical Society, Phil Mollon is also a clinical psychologist and trained in psychotherapy at the Tavistock Clinic. He works primarily within the NHS. With several books published, his interests have included Kohut and Self Psychology, trauma and traumatic memory, dissociative states of mind, shame, and disturbances in the experience of self. He is on the Advisory Board of the New York Institute for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology. In addition, Mollon is an advanced practitioner of meridian energy therapies, an accredited practitioner of EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) and a licensed trainer of Emotrance™ (an energy therapy). His latest book serves as an introduction to the psychoanalytic field of the methods of treatment in energy psychology and the treatment for trauma, EMDR, all of which have developed over the last 25 years. With a range of case illustrations, mostly brief and from NHS clinics, the book shows how these treatment methods allow the rapid release and processing of painful emotions and traumatic memories. Mollon compares the pioneers of these methods with the pioneers of psychoanalysis. Indeed the book shows how they are compatible with many of the original insights of Freudian psychoanalysis. Trauma, he writes, ‘hijacks the body’ and ‘acts as if it were a wish’ (p. 36), and he explains why he thinks attention should be paid to the way emotion and trauma are experienced within the patient. Discussing Freud's thoughts on how internal conflict is akin to traumatic experience and how remembering is replaced by repeating, he suggests the focused targeting and processing of specific emotions could be usefully combined with, and enhance, the lengthy, unstructured work of ‘psychoanalytic enquiry’ (p. xv).

EMDR was originally developed by clinical psychologist Francine Shapiro.

Jonathan Smith  

The appearance of this new book on managing psychological therapies in primary care comes at a crucial moment in the development of counselling and psychotherapy in primary care in the NHS. It is a moment when, looking back over the last 15 to 20 years, one can conclude that much has been achieved. Psychological therapies have clearly established their place as a key component of mental health service delivery at a primary care level. It is also a moment of transition, for as the authors note the days of the independent self-employed practitioner are over. The requirements of clinical governance and equity of access to services, to minimize postal code determination of the quality of service provision, means that the structured management of counselling services across PCTs or Mental Health Trusts has become unavoidable. Such a period of transition creates new challenges and opportunities. It is also potentially a moment of considerable risk that the whole endeavour to establish flexible humane counselling services in the primary care setting may become shipwrecked on the wind of bureaucratization and over-simplification.

The authors of this book are seasoned practitioners who possess a wealth of experience in management and in acting as consultants to both counsellors and managers working in primary care. Joan Foster is Chair of the National Association of Counsellors and Psychotherapists in Primary Care and Antonia Murphy worked as co-ordinator of the Southern Derbyshire Health Authority managed counselling service. Between them they have written a book in a very engaging and often witty style on a subject which might otherwise seem rather dry and technical. They are able to do this because they possess a clear knowledge and appreciation of the history and current context in which the development of counselling in primary care has taken place. They have been at the forefront of the emergence of this branch of the profession, and their book reflects their own enthusiasm, vision, energy and commitment to primary care counselling. This has evidently been rooted in the hard graft of creatively working on the coal-face, struggling to find solutions to the many complexities that present themselves to the practitioner and manager in this setting, in the context of swirling organizational changes within the NHS itself.

The aim of this paper is to set out in sequence the evolution of Meltzer's ideas and the influence on them of Bion's. It has been the combination of his own explorations of the intrusive form of projective identification with the non-intrusive form in Bion's theory of thinking and with his theory of groups that came to define for Meltzer the essence of two of the three Post-Kleinian metapsychologies: ‘geographical and epistemological’ while in Bion's theory of affects he found the key to a third: the ‘aesthetic’.

London

Gertrud Mander  

Emigration, exile and multilingualism, the subjects of this marvellous book, are central issues of our time and, as I am an emigrant myself, they are very close to my heart. So much so that some time ago, after 20 years of practising psychotherapy in London, I started a group with colleagues who, like me, came from Germany and were bilingual. We were all trained in English and mostly worked in English, although all of us occasionally spoke German with a German patient, were reading Freud in German and were interested in the question, whether psychotherapy should be given in the mother tongue, and was second-best only if experienced in an acquired language. I had had three English therapists and I had always worked in English, even with German patients, except for one case. I had switched over to writing in English, though in my first profession as a journalist I had written in German, but I was now at last asking myself why I was avoiding my mother tongue and what was the difference when I spoke or worked in one language rather than the other? Discussing these questions in the group led to an exciting exploration of what we felt about being emigrants, of being in exile but, with one exception, not refugees.

Reading the book Lost Childhood and the Language of Exile confronted me again powerfully with all these questions, and significantly deepened the ideas that had come up in our German group. It opened up the added issues of multilingualism, multiculturalism, loss of country and childhood. It tapped into the knowledge that the history of psychoanalysis is a history of exile and migration, of translation, of trying to find a promised land and an identity, of working with lost childhoods, and relating to strangers and to others. Freud in old age was, like Moses, migrating to a promised land, where the work he had written in his German mother tongue had been translated into an English Standard Edition that would disseminate it all over the world and create an international analytic community.

London

Linda Pethick  

This collection of papers offers the opportunity to engage with the neuroscientific issues that are now so relevant to psychoanalysis. It brings together some current psychoanalytic, attachment, neuropsychological and psycho-biological perspectives on emotional development, hence the subtitle of the book Creating Connections. It offers an introduction to current developments in these different fields of research on emotional development and is a wide-ranging and useful book that well repays the effort of reading it.

The book is divided into two sections, the first contains four papers by writers pre-eminent in the field of neuroscience and attachment theory. All have written in more extensive detail elsewhere but these papers offer excellent, comprehensive introductions to the work of Schore, Solms and Turnbull in neuroscience, a useful summary by Miriam Steele of current developments in research on attachment theory and a paper by Peter Fonagy which addresses the claim that genetics determine psychological problems. The second section provides a clinical perspective on development, with six papers on patients within different age ranges from infancy to adulthood with problematical development issues.

Allan Schore's ‘The human unconscious: the development of the right brain and its role in early emotional life’ is a dense and fascinating paper. It presents an overview of recent psychological studies of the social-emotional development of infants and neurobiological research on the maturation of the early developing right brain. Schore describes the early development of the right hemisphere of the brain with particular reference to its link to attachment. Neurobiology has established that the infant brain ‘is designed to be moulded by the environment it encounters’ (p. 24), which means that early socio-emotional experiences influence the maturation of the biological structure of the brain. The early attachment relationship of the infant ‘powerfully affects the structure of the brain’, and these attachment experiences indelibly impact the trajectory of emotional development, the ongoing maturational potential, over the course of the life span (p. 26). This is something with which we are familiar theoretically and clinically given a biological basis.

International Forum of Psychoanalysis14, 134-137, 2005

Perversion - Drive, Object and Jouissance

Carlos Antǒnio Andrade Mello, Maria Lúcia de Salvo Coimbra, Maria Luiza Arrojado Lisboa, Maria Luisa Duarte Vilela and Stella Maris Anchieta

The way the drive (Trieb) is lived by the subject in a singular manner identifies the different clinical structures: neurosis, psychosis and perversion. The perverse in his act is determined by the categorical imperative ‘jouissance’: he/she lives for the jouissance; he/she struggles to take possession of it, to organize it and to prolong it (to extend it). Desire, in the perversion, does not emerge as a question about the desire of the Other, as it does in neurosis. It makes its presence as a hard and inflexible response under the form of will of jouissance. What about the real of jouissance in psychoanalysis? How would the analyst listen to the perverse?



International Forum of Psychoanalysis14, 176-182, 2005

Perversion on the other Side of the Couch

Paulo Ceccarelli

Taking as his starting point the fact that, according to Freudian theory, perversion is inherent to the human being, the author focuses upon an aspect of perversion that has been little discussed: perversion on the other side of the couch, and thereby questions of how, in psychoanalytic theoretical and clinical practice, perverted drive motions may be presented. Such a phenomenon takes various forms: actually being enacted with patients; using psychoanalytic theory as a normative rule; the individual choice of profession and so forth. To exemplify his point of view, the author presents four different expressions of sexuality in Freudian theory: genital sexuality, perverted sexuality, the sexuality of the Ideals and narcissistic sexuality. After differentiating these four sexual expressions, the author shows how each of them may generate perversion in both clinical and theoretical psychoanalysis.



International Forum of Psychoanalysis15, 19-33, 2006

In Dialogue with Daniel Stern: A Review and Discussion of the Present Moment in Psychotherapy and Everyday Life

Lennart Ramberg

Daniel Stern's concepts of ‘present moment’ and ‘now moment’, with impending kairos, are described. In the latter, the patient demands the authentic presence of the analyst. If the analyst can open himself to the patient, he proposes that this will result in more profound changes in the patient's implicit knowing than verbal interpretations in the narrative domain would lead to. The value of intersubjectively relating and dwelling more in the phenomenal than in the narrative dimension is highlighted. A similarity to the works of the existential psychoanalyst Harold Kelman is shown. The author agrees with, but also problematizes, a tendency to favour the implicit, devaluing verbal understanding and interpretation, which may result in the patient not seeing the primitive levels in his inner life. For this purpose, works from D.W. Winnicott, Jessica Benjamin and Christopher Bollas, as well as others, are used. The author concludes that object relations and intersubjective theory need to complement each other; further that there is a need to give words to the middle-ground between the phenomenal and narrative dimensions.

Francis Grier

Flat 1, 5 St Cuthbert's Road, London NW2 3QJ. [email: grier@globalnet.co.uk]

Francis Grier  

This paper is about the unconscious ideals couples share, and the dynamic effect of these on their relationships. With the aid of two detailed clinical examples, I examine how the unconscious ideals actually affecting couples' relationships are often quite different from couples' conscious ideas of their ideals, and, in particular, how couples can get fixated in paranoid-schizoid and regressive shared states of mind as a result. I explore the kind of psychological journey couples typically find they have to tread if they are to develop to ideals which are more rational and tolerant, borne of the depressive position. I note how couples' notions of betrayal and forgiveness are quite different according to whether they are relating from the paranoid-schizoid or depressive position.

Some Thoughts on Schreber (and Freud): Depression, Paranoia and A Delusional System

Sue Gottlieb

Sue Gottlieb

Babbs Farm, Westhill Lane, Basonbridge, Highbridge, Somerset TA9 4RF

Sue Gottlieb  

Freud's paper on Daniel Paul Schreber is a seminal psychoanalytic text (Freud 1911). In it, he sets out his argument that Schreber's paranoid delusions arose from repressed homosexuality. This paper reconsiders the case of Schreber from a contemporary perspective chiefly by studying, as did Freud, Schreber's autobiographical Memoirs of My Nervous Illness (Schreber 1903), but also by drawing upon more recent biographical information. It follows the view put forward by Lothane (1992), and recently elaborated by Steiner (2004), that Schreber's illness was originally depressive in nature, and then progressed to paranoia and finally to a settled delusional system. It reviews many of Freud's insights, contending that although some, such as his understanding of the mechanism of paranoia and the manner by which a delusion of persecution is converted into a religious delusion of grandeur, have stood the test of time, others, such as the causal relationship he proposes between homosexuality and paranoia, do not.

Joanna Ryan  

The absence of frameworks for discussion of social class issues within psychotherapy is one concern of this exploratory paper. Another is to raise questions about how we might think psychoanalytically about the far-reaching impact of class. A small exploratory qualitative research study is described in which experienced psychoanalytic psychotherapists were interviewed about class issues. The interviews mainly concerned their perceptions and understandings of class issues within psychotherapeutic relationships, but were framed by biographical and professional experiences relating to class. The reports from pairings of differently classed therapists and patients raised many questions about the ways in which class and class differences can be experienced and understood within the transference/countertransference matrix, as well as the surrounding anxieties and projections.

This paper considers Freud's concept of trauma and its resonances in contemporary cultural discourse, focusing on the complex temporality and the unknowable dimension of traumatic experience. The paper traces the shifting emphasis from Freud's initial intent to discover the original traumatic event, towards accepting the indeterminacy of what can be known in this experience. It is suggested that this psychoanalytic understanding of trauma provides a key perspective for considering the problematic issue of representation of ‘real’ events in the broader cultural domain. The approach to trauma discussed in this paper offers a framework in which it is possible to allow multiple interpretations and shifting perspectives on events, to stay open to unknowable dimensions, and at the same time to accept the presence of layers from the past. Lastly, the impact of Freud's insights on trauma on historical, literary and cinematic discourse is explored through discussing a few examples in detail.

This paper suggests that the prohibition against ‘taking the role of the good object’ may inhibit therapists from an appropriate recognition of a loving relation between the patient and themselves. It is argued that the prohibition actually refers to a defensive attempt to get the analyst to take the role of the idealized object as a defence against the emergence of bad objects in the transference. This clinical scenario is contrasted with one where the patient needs to find in their therapist a real good object who genuinely cares for them.

Negative Therapeutic Reaction

Kate Tindle

Kate Tindle

5th floor, Crawford House, Precinct Centre, Oxford Road, Manchester M13 9QS. [email: kate.tindle@manchester.ac.uk]

Kate Tindle  

For the last 80 years the term ‘negative therapeutic reaction’ has been used by psychoanalysts and psychotherapists to define the phenomenon of improvement followed by deterioration of a client's psychological or symptomatic condition, apparently in response to their therapist's interventions. Negative therapeutic reaction has been the subject of many papers written by these practitioners, who in various ways have attempted to clarify and understand what goes wrong in such therapeutic encounters.

This paper summarises the ideas of many psychoanalytic writers and practitioners who have worked throughout the span of the twentieth century, and up to the present day. Various aspects of negative therapeutic reaction are explored, such as alternative definitions of the concept, possible origins of NTR, the impact of the therapeutic relationship, and treatment implications. These ideas are compared and discussed, drawing mainly on the object relations theories of Fairbairn (1943), and illustrated through examples from myth, literature, research and clinical vignettes.

Gavin Ivey  

How the Oedipus complex is organized and experienced is determined by what we do in our minds with the presence of the other perceived to come between us and our objects. Various oedipal models have mapped various configurations of three-ness: psychic patterns of self in relation to a couple. These configurations are determined by how, and at what level, we struggle with the problematic presence of a third person. The application of Freudian and Kleinian oedipal models to case material from an adult male patient is used to illustrate the complexity and layering of oedipal issues, and the importance of keeping various oedipal perspectives in mind in the course of our analytic work. The paper concludes by differentiating my patient from those manifesting triadic aversion or hatred of three-ness. The latter not only describes a problematic category of analytic patient, but throws into stark relief the more ‘mature’ oedipal configurations corresponding to Freud's and Klein's oedipal models.
